name: Tod

(Glottolog ref 472417 lists the same chapter as D. D. Sharma 1992, 'Tod (Stod)', in Tribal Languages of Himachal Pradesh: Part One, Studies in Tibeto-Himalayan Languages II, Mittal Publications, pp. 261-346, description type, language code 'Tod (Stod) = Stod Bhoti [sbu]'; verified)
catalog_locator: Tod chapter, sec. 1.3.5 'Syllabic division', book p. 279 (CL-CSKHPKV-15657; layout). Supporting: sec. 1.1.4(i) p. 266 and sec. 7.2.5 p. 334.
catalog_quote: The number of trisyllabic words is limited in it and there are no quadrisyllabic words too in it. Dissyllabic and polysyllabic words are both, mono-morphomic and poly-morphomic. 1.3.5. Syllabic division: In a disyllabic word the initial syllable bears a higher accent, consequently, it is clearly kept apart from the succeeding syllable. As such the syllabic division is clearly maintained, even in the case of syllabic sequences, e.g. /pi-ši/ cat, /kye-ti/ armpit, /me-bu/ glow worm, /no-cuṅ/ younger brother, /cin-te/ heavy, /ə-u/ husband, /ra-o/ hoof. /še-i/ mustard, /ul-thuṅ/ necklace. /men-toʔg/ flower. ... In poly-syllabic words, the syllabic entity of the first two syllables is, fully maintained due to higher accent on them but it is considerably reduced in the last one, as in /pho-so-cən/ proud, /cha-mo-ce/ grand-daughter, /pin-ki-tiʔg/ lizard, etc.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the initial syllable of disyllables; in trisyllabic words (the longest native type) the first two syllables are prominent and the final syllable is reduced. Accented vowels in open syllables are phonetically lengthened (p. 266). Accent is treated as non-contrastive (no accent/tone section is given for Tod, unlike the neighbouring Pattani and Gahri chapters of the same book).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such; for trisyllables the author says the first two syllables both carry 'higher accent' relative to a reduced final syllable, without ranking them.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The remark is made incidentally in the syllabification section, not as a formal stress rule; no discussion of compounds, suffixed verb forms or loanwords. Sec. 7.2.5 (p. 334) separately notes utterance-level emphatic 'stress/pitch accent' on a syllable of the emphasized word.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms (mono-, di- and trisyllabic lexical words; author states there are no quadrisyllabic words). Note older Lahul-based observation by Jaeschke 1867 p. 153 (West Tibetan border provinces generally): stress usually on the root/stem syllable, but in compounds more often on the last member — consistent with initial accent on simplex words but suggesting compound-final prominence, which Sharma does not address. Roerich 1933 instead describes four tonemes for Lahul Tibetan and says nothing about stress position; LSI 1909 says tones are 'hardly used'.
new_statements.identity_note: Sharma's 'Tod' is the Tibetan variety of the upper Bhaga valley (Kwaring to Darcha; informants from Rang-yo near Darcha and Teeno/Tinno), i.e. the Stod/Kolong dialect proper of Stod Bhoti (stod1241). Roerich 1933 and LSI 1909 'Lahul dialect' cover both the Kolong (sTod-skad) and Koksar (Khoksar) sub-dialects, both subsumed under stod1241. Jaeschke 1867's accent remark is about the West Tibetan border provinces generally (observer based at Kyelang, Lahul), not Stod specifically. The LSI-Himachal Pradesh 2023 'Lahauli (= Stod-Bhoti)' chapter uses Udaipur-tehsil data that look like Pattani (Manchad, patt1248) and should not be used for stod1241; its 'Bhotia' chapter is Spiti Bhoti (spit1240).

sources.locator: Tod chapter, sec. 1.3.5 'Syllabic division', p. 279 (p. 297 of the archive.org scan CL-CSKHPKV-15657); supporting remark sec. 1.1.4(i), p. 266
sources.note: The Tod chapter has no dedicated accent/suprasegmental section (the Pattani and Gahri chapters do). The only positional statement is in 1.3.5 'Syllabic division', p. 279: in a disyllabic word the initial syllable bears a higher accent; in polysyllabic (trisyllabic) words the first two syllables carry higher accent and the last is considerably reduced. p. 266: accented vowels at the end of an open syllable are realized comparatively long. p. 334 (7.2.5): emphatic stress/pitch accent on a syllable of the emphasized word in utterances. No mention of tone for Tod.

sources.citation: Jaeschke, H. A. 1867. Über die Phonetik der tibetischen Sprache. Monatsberichte der Königlich Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin 1867, Nachtrag (vorgelegt 1 Nov. 1866), pp. 148 ff.
sources.note: p. 153, describing the present pronunciation of the 'westliche Gränzprovinzen' (Jaeschke lived ten years at Kyelang, Lahul): vowels short in closed or unstressed open syllables, somewhat longer in stressed open syllables; 'Betont sind, wie im Deutschen, gewöhnlich die Wurzel- oder Stammsylben; in Compositis jedoch häufiger die letzte als die erste.' General West-Tibetan statement, not tied to Stod specifically.

sources.citation: Language Division, Office of the Registrar General, India. 2023. Linguistic Survey of India: Himachal Pradesh. 'Lahauli' chapter by Dipshikha Bose & J. C. Sharma (pp. 951 ff.); 'Bhotia' chapter by S. Ganesh Baskaran (pp. 1013 ff.).
sources.note: 'Lahauli' chapter says Lahauli is 'also known as Stod-Bhoti' but its data were collected in Udaipur tehsil/Kullu and look Pattani-like (identity doubtful); suprasegmentals listed as nasalization, length and tone ('Lahuli is a tonal language'), stress only named in a garbled list, no positional rule. 'Bhotia' chapter is Spiti fieldwork (spit1240): three contrastive tones, no stress rule. Silent on Stod word stress.

sources.citation: Roerich, George N. de. 1933. The Tibetan dialect of Lahul (Tibetica I; Journal of Urusvati Himalayan Research Institute 3: 83-189). Covers Lahul Tibetan: Kolong 'Tod-kad' (sTod-skad, upper Bhaga) and Koksar sub-dialects.
sources.note: Phonology has a 'Tones' section: Lahul Tibetan 'possesses four tonemes' (high rising, high even, low even, falling abrupt), conditioned by initial voicing and lost finals. No statement on the position of word stress; 'strong stress' is mentioned only for the articulation of word-initial velar nasal.

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. (ed; Konow) 1909. Linguistic Survey of India, vol. III part I (Tibeto-Burman family), 'Lahul dialect' pp. 69-71, with Jaeschke's 1866 specimen.
sources.note: p. 70: 'Tones are hardly used in the dialect' (abrupt tone from dropped finals only). No rule stated, but p. 70-71: 'The stress has been indicated by putting a ´ above the accented syllable' in Jaeschke's specimen; the marks fall mostly on the first (root) syllable (Dí-ka', gyál-po, lón-po, chhén-po, dán-pa, sém-chan, lég-pa, tsái-te) and on the second member in compounds/derived forms (nyan-yó', gyal-jé', Sal-gyál-la, ja'-zúg, pe-já').
